WoW: Forever

WoW: Forever class guides

Levelling guides for all nine classes in World of Warcraft: Forever, which relaunches the 1–60 game on November 4, 2026, with everyone starting from scratch on the same day.

Class guidesProfession guides

WoW: Forever · Updated October 5, 2026 · Beta build 1.60.1.70124 · Null Ossuary

These are levelling guides. Forever's beta is capped at level 30 as of the October 1 build, raised from 20 that day, there is no raid testing, and item stats stay hidden until something drops. No level-60 build, best-in-slot list or class ranking for Forever exists yet. We checked the three sites these guides are compiled from: ClassicWoW.gg publishes the complete level-60 talent trees and a calculator, and says of them "this is the full tree, not a suggested build"; Icy Veins' tier-list directory lists every tier list as "COMING SOON"; Wowhead's class guides stop at level 20. A level-60 ranking found elsewhere was not read off a tested character.

What we can state confidently: talent trees, ability training levels and spell changes, all taken from foreverchanges.pro's reading of the beta client. What is firmer still is anything Blizzard has published directly. Raids open December 9, five weeks after launch, and we will write the endgame half then. Blizzard has begun publishing official class deep dives, and they outrank every guide site: Priest, Warrior, Hunter and Druid are covered as of September 30, 2026, and those four pages are written from Blizzard's own text. The other five are not yet covered, and Blizzard's own caveat applies throughout: "class abilities and talents may continue to evolve throughout the beta test and are subject to additional changes."

Where the verdicts come from

Every evaluative claim on these pages belongs to someone. Spec and class verdicts are read off the three guide sites — Wowhead, Icy Veins and ClassicWoW.gg — and off Blizzard's own posts, which outrank all three wherever they say anything. Where those sources agree, we say so. Where they disagree, the page names which said what rather than quietly picking a winner. Where only one of them scores something, we say that too. And where we worked something out ourselves — an extended talent build, a judgement no source makes — it carries the marker (ours, not a source's). We do not issue our own verdict and leave it reading like a fact. And we do not rank the specs for you at all: a spec is introduced by what it is for and what it is strongest at, because best and worst depend on whether you are questing alone or standing in a group.

Mechanics are a different matter and are stated flatly: talent trees, training levels and numbers come from the beta client and from Blizzard directly, not from anyone's opinion.

Everyone is new on November 4

There is no back catalogue to catch up on, nothing to unlock first and no established players with a head start. If you have never played WoW, our own view is that there has not been a better moment in twenty years to start.

Each class guide below is written for levelling from 1 to 60, opens with a short section for players new to that class, and says plainly where something is unknown rather than guessing.

The three roles

Group content is built around three jobs. You do not have to choose now, but the words come up constantly.

RoleWhat you actually doPer five-person group
TankHold the monsters' attention so they hit you instead of everyone else, and survive itOne
HealerKeep everyone alive, mostly by watching health bars rather than the fightOne
DPSDeal damage and kill thingsThree

Some classes do only one of these. Some do all three, though never at once — you switch by respending talent points and changing gear.

Because groups need three DPS and only one of each other role, DPS is the most common thing to be and the hardest to get invited as. Tanks and healers get invited instantly. There is no automatic group finder in Forever, so grouping means asking.

"Best for levelling" almost always means "best for soloing"

This is the most important thing on the page, and every guide site gets it wrong by omission.

When a guide rates a spec for levelling, it is nearly always rating how fast it kills things by itself. That is a real question, and it is not the only one. Levelling in groups and dungeons is a different activity, and the specs that rate worst for soloing, healers especially, are often the ones that reach 60 with the least waiting, because a healer never sits in a queue.

Forever sharpened that distinction by paying dungeon quest experience above normal quest values — then pulled half of that back on October 1, when Blizzard cut the extra experience from dungeon quests by 50%, saying directly that it was responding to feedback on levelling speed. A dungeon route is still a deliberate design rather than a workaround; it is simply worth less than it was before that build, and this is the number most likely to move again before launch.

So the pages below do not rank the specs against each other. Each one says what its spec is for and what it is strongest at. The guide sites' levelling scores are still reported, on the spec pages where there is room to say what they measure — solo kill speed, and nothing else. Every spec in the game can reach level 60. None of them is a trap.

Where it matters most:

If you mostlyThen
Quest aloneThe levelling scores on the spec pages are measuring the right thing for you
Run dungeonsIgnore those scores. Healers and tanks wait least for a group
Play with a friendAlmost anything works. Pick what you want to play at 60

Which class should you pick?

Honestly, the one whose fantasy appeals. Every class finishes the levelling game solo, and the differences below change how it feels far more than whether you succeed. No source ranks the nine classes against each other for Forever yet — Icy Veins' tier lists all read "COMING SOON" — so the rows below are role facts — which class can do which job — and nothing more.

If you want to…Consider
Be hard to kill and hold the lineWarrior, Paladin, Druid
Keep people alivePriest, Paladin, Shaman, Druid
Kill things from a distanceMage, Warlock, Hunter, Shaman, Priest, Druid
Kill things up closeRogue, Warrior, Paladin, Shaman, Druid

Two things worth knowing before you commit. Warrior's Rage economy is still moving: Blizzard's own September 30 Class Deep Dive concedes Rage-generation bugs it is still tracking down, and a critical strike now gives 100% increased Rage. This attack deals 50% weapon damage plus 26 and immobilizes the target for 5 sec. Professions

Profession guides are here: all twelve, plus the two systems Forever added.

Three things worth knowing before you pick:

  • Take Cooking at level 1. 103 of its dishes give +5% experience from kills, and the first one works at skill 1 on a level-1 character. It costs you no primary slot.
  • Only the six crafting professions earn Legacy Points. None of the three gathering professions earns any of the 18 on offer, so a gathering pair earns you nothing.
  • Camping is new, and it lets a group hand itself class buffs it does not have.

What is new in Forever

Beyond the new zones and dungeons, these change how you level whatever you pick. The first three moved in the October 1 build, so they are what a guide written last week has wrong.

  • Dungeons pay in quests, not in kills. Dungeon quest experience is paid above normal quest values — then cut by 50% on October 1, so that bonus is now half what it was. A matching cut to kill experience inside dungeons is widely repeated, and Blizzard has published no number for it: that is the client reading, not an official figure. Run each dungeon once for its quests rather than repeating it, and expect the quest number to keep moving: Blizzard is openly tuning levelling speed during the beta.
  • Fourteen dungeons are open at the level-30 cap, and three of them arrived on October 1: Excavation Site: Wetlands (26–31), Razorfen Downs (25+) and Uldaman (30+), alongside the eleven already available: Ragefire Chasm, Hall of Thanes, Ruins of Lordaeron, Wailing Caverns, the Deadmines, Shadowfang Keep, the Stockade, Blackfathom Deeps, Gnomeregan, Razorfen Kraul and Scarlet Monastery.
  • A low-rank spell is no longer a free efficiency trick. Casting a rank well below your level now gets less from your Spell Damage and Spell Healing and has a reduced chance to trigger your own talents. Blizzard's example: a rank 1 Frostbolt at level 60 has a 0% chance to proc FrostbiteFrostbiteTalentCastInstant. Downranking to save mana now costs you procs, so it is a decision rather than a habit.
  • Talent points can eventually start earlier than 10. But not on your first character. The account-wide Legacy system has a perk, TalentedTalentedTalentCastInstantYou gain talent points every level starting at level 5 instead of starting at level 10, but you still may not have more than 51 total talent points.: five ranks, each moving your first talent point one level earlier, from 10 down to 5. It costs ten Legacy Points — five ranks of Well RestedWell RestedTalentCastInstantYour rested experience accumulates 20% faster and your rested experience cap is increased by 20%. first, then five of its own, and Legacy Points are earned one per challenge, such as levelling a class to 25, 45 or 60, or a profession to 150, 225 or 300. A brand-new account on November 4 has none. The 51-point total at 60 never changes; the perk only moves when the points arrive, and at full rank a level-30 character holds 26 points instead of 21.
  • Six new race and class combinations: Gnome Priest, Human Hunter, Dwarf Shaman, Orc Mage, Troll Warlock and Undead Paladin. Paladin and Shaman are no longer faction-locked. Blizzard says more combinations are planned.
  • There is a tenth race. The Skyborne are neutral, playable on either faction, with their own starting area in the Zephras Isles, and they play Druid, Hunter, Rogue and Warrior on both sides, Mage on Alliance only and Shaman on Horde only. The race and its starting experience need an optional upgrade purchase, so this is the one class-and-race choice on this page that costs money.
  • Every race now carries four racials, two active and two passive, and the familiar names often do something different. Do not pick from a Classic racial ranking.
  • Every one of the 27 talent trees gained a fourth one-point ability at 16 points, alongside the existing 11, 21 and 31-point talents. Talents that merely improved a class buff, such as Blessing of Kings and Improved Mark of the Wild, were removed, because those improvements are baseline now. Divine Spirit went the same way for a different reason: it was the buff itself rather than an improvement to one, and it is now baseline to every Priest, learned at level 30.
  • Dual Specialization arrives at level 40, so from 40 you carry two talent builds and swap between them instead of paying to respec. Blizzard states this in both class deep dives. For a hybrid — a Druid, Paladin, Priest, Shaman or Warrior — it is the level the class stops being one job at a time.
  • Talents are changed at a class trainer in a major city, Legacy talents included. There is no respec-anywhere.
  • Hit and critical strike are combined across melee, ranged and spells, and healing gear also grants some bonus damage. One stat line now serves a whole character, which is why weapon and gear advice on these pages differs from Classic's.
  • Weapon-specialisation racials became critical-strike racials, and they work off an equipped weapon rather than one you swing, so weapon type is now worth a thought even for casters.

The levelling pace itself is unchanged from Classic. Expect to walk a great deal before your mount, to drink after fights if you use mana, and for dying to cost time rather than progress.
